Complementary qualitative analysis further highlighted a critical trade-off: perceived efficiency gains were weighed against major concerns related to algorithmic bias, hallucinations, and data confidentiality. The findings offer fine-grained empirical evidence on how researchers respond to different forms of LLM involvement in peer review, yielding actionable implications for journals and publishers while emphasizing the responsible integration of LLMs.

title: Assessing and comparing the coverage of publications of six Italian universities in OpenCitations
abstract: Abstract Recent initiatives advocating responsible, transparent research assessment have intensified the call to use open research information rather than proprietary databases. This study evaluates the coverage and citation representation of publications recorded in the Current Research Information Systems (CRIS), all instances of the IRIS software platform, of six Italian universities within OpenCitations, a community-owned open infrastructure. Using persistent identifiers (DOIs, PMIDs, and ISBNs) specified in the IRIS installations involved, we matched the publications recorded in OpenCitations Meta and extracted the related citation links from the OpenCitations Index. Results show that OpenCitations covers, on average, over 40% of IRIS publications, which is quantitatively comparable to those reported by Scopus and Web of Science in another study. However, gaps persist, particularly for publication types prevalent in the Social Sciences and Humanities, such as monographs and critical editions. Overall, the findings demonstrate the growing maturity of OpenCitations and, more broadly, of Open Science infrastructures as viable alternatives as sources of research information, while highlighting areas where further metadata enrichment and interoperability efforts are needed.

title: Presence and visibility of local journals in international scientific databases
abstract: This work is part of the COMPARE project (Ref: PID2020-117007RA-I00) funded by the Spanish Ministry of Science (Ref: MCIN/AEI/10.13039/501100011033 FSE invierte en tu futuro). Victoria Di Césare is currently supported by a FPI grant from the Spanish Ministry of Science (Ref: PRE2021-097022). Nicolas Robinson-Garcia is currently supported by a Ramón y Cajal grant from the Spanish Ministry of Science (Ref: RYC2019-027886-I).

title: LLM-assisted writing and citation advantage: evidence from scientific publications before and after ChatGPT release
abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence has become a routine part of academic writing. While much of the debate has focused on questions of integrity and authorship, less attention has been paid to how AI-assisted writing may affect research evaluation itself. This paper asks a straightforward but important question: does the use of LLMs in academic writing change how scientific work is rewarded once it enters the citation system, even when the underlying research is legitimate? We study this question using a large-scale dataset that combines arXiv records with bibliometric information from Crossref, covering 234,073 research papers published between 2019 and 2025. To identify likely AI involvement, we train a text classification model on pre-LLM human-written abstracts and AI-generated rewrites, allowing us to detect stylistic features associated with LLM-assisted writing. We then examine how predicted LLM usage relates to citation outcomes using two complementary strategies: regression models with rich controls and fixed effects, and a counterfactual machine learning approach that compares observed citations to levels predicted from 2021–2022 citation patterns. Across both analyses, papers whose abstracts show signs of LLM-assisted writing receive more citations than otherwise similar papers. Specifically, papers classified as potentially written with the aid of LLMs exhibit approximately 7.04% higher citation counts on average ( p < 0.01) relative to non-LLM papers. This difference remains after accounting for journal characteristics, collaboration size, reference lists, abstract length, and authors’ prior citation records, and it exceeds what would be expected based on historical citation dynamics alone. The results suggest that AI-assisted writing confers a modest but systematic advantage in visibility and discoverability that translates into higher measured impact. Rather than pointing to misconduct, these findings highlight a structural shift in how research is evaluated. As writing itself becomes easier to optimize through AI, citation-based indicators increasingly capture differences in presentation as well as differences in scientific contribution. The study therefore calls for greater caution in interpreting bibliometric measures in an academic environment where text is no longer produced solely by human authors.

title: Mission-oriented scientometrics: a data-driven framework for assessing national readiness and alignment in strategic innovation missions
abstract: Mission-oriented innovation policies have become a central strategy for addressing complex societal challenges, yet empirical tools capable of evaluating national readiness and alignment with mission priorities remain underdeveloped. This study develops a multidimensional mission-oriented scientometrics framework designed to assess how effectively national science, technology, and innovation (STI) systems mobilize research and technological capabilities toward strategic missions. The framework integrates bibliometric indicators, patent analytics, thematic convergence analysis, and collaboration network structures to capture multidimensional patterns of alignment across scientific output, technological trajectories, and institutional interactions. Using global data on clean energy transition, climate adaptation, and advanced health technologies, the study examines national performance across selected countries from 2010 to 2023. The results show that countries with distributed, cross-sectoral collaboration networks exhibit stronger thematic convergence toward mission priorities, while those with coherent linkages between scientific publications and patenting activity demonstrate more rapid translation of research into mission-related technologies. The findings highlight the critical importance of governance quality, policy coherence, institutional complementarity, and sustained R&D investment in shaping mission readiness. The proposed scientometric framework offers a scalable and replicable tool for policymakers seeking to monitor mission-oriented transitions, identify systemic bottlenecks, and design evidence-based STI strategies. By integrating quantitative scientometric methods with mission-oriented policy perspectives, this study contributes an empirical framework for supporting evidence-informed STI policy analysis and mission-oriented evaluation.

title: Understanding prolonged retraction lag among retracted biomedical papers: an explainable machine-learning analysis
abstract: Retractions are vital for scientific self-correction, yet prolonged lags between publication and retraction allow flawed papers to persist in the literature and distort future research through citations. Here, we applied explainable machine learning to identify the key factors associated with prolonged retraction lags in biomedical papers. Using 13,685 biomedical papers that were ultimately retracted, we classify whether the observed publication-to-retraction interval exceeded a practically meaningful three-year threshold, distinguishing between relatively short and prolonged retraction lag. LightGBM achieved the highest F1-score and performance comparable to Random Forest and XGBoost in discrimination and calibration; therefore, it was selected as the primary model for SHAP-based interpretation. SHAP analysis results show that papers published by Hindawi were associated with relatively short retraction lag, a pattern that may reflect differences in publication volume, post-publication scrutiny, and research-integrity oversight environments rather than superior correction efficiency. SJR score showed a nonlinear association with prolonged retraction lag, while moderate levels of retraction reason complexity were generally associated with a higher predicted likelihood of prolonged retraction lag. The academic age Gini coefficient shows an inverted U-shaped association with retraction lag, with moderate levels associated with higher predicted likelihoods of prolonged lag. Prolonged retraction lags typically resulted from the cumulative interaction of multiple factors, whereas relatively short retraction lags were more often characterized by a simpler and more concentrated predictive structure. These results highlight the importance of institutional publishing contexts in shaping retraction timeliness and provide practical insights for research-integrity governance. These associations are conditional on eventual retraction and should be interpreted as retrospective evidence about variation in retraction timeliness, rather than as an early-warning model for the broader population of published papers.

title: Hunting grounds for predatory publishers
abstract: Abstract Are some preprint platforms more attractive to predatory publishers than others? To explore this question, we analyze unsolicited messages received for a research paper spanning the social and health sciences. The paper was posted on two major preprint platforms: Research Square, which primarily serves the natural and health sciences, and the Social Science Research Network (SSRN), the leading platform for social sciences. Using an identification strategy that attributes differences in solicitation volume to platform-specific factors rather than the study’s characteristics, authors, or institutions, we find significant differences in the volume of predatory solicitations. Research Square received considerably more solicitations, mostly from non-social science disciplines such as clinical medicine and psychiatry. This suggests that predatory publishers not only target Research Square more frequently but are also attracted to disciplines with higher publication pressure and greater commercial potential. These findings provide researchers with a clearer understanding of the risks associated with different platforms and offer insights into avoiding predatory publishers.

title: Quantifying scholars’ marginal contributions to average-based journal metrics
abstract: Abstract Attributing journal metrics to individual scholars is essential for modeling research influence, yet current methods rely on a restrictive assumption of monotonicity. Traditional credit allocation frameworks, such as Full and Fractional counting, assume that adding a research article to a portfolio never decreases a scholar’s attributed standing. While valid for cumulative metrics, this logic is mathematically inconsistent with average-based metrics like the Journal Impact Factor (JIF). Such indicators are inherently non-monotonic functions where performance below the established mean exerts a reductive impact on the aggregate score. This study challenges the monotonic baseline by introducing a marginal attribution framework that captures how individual marginal contributions can either increase or decrease an average-based journal metric. We propose three novel methods: Marginal Full Credit , Marginal Fractional Credit , and Marginal Shapley . The latter adapts the game-theoretic Shapley value using an average-based characteristic function to calculate marginal contributions that may be negative. To ensure scalability for large datasets where exact computation is prohibitively complex, we employ a statistically rigorous and commonly used bounded Monte Carlo approximation. Empirically, we test these methods on a dataset of articles from twelve leading Information Science journals. Our findings demonstrate that, because citation distributions are highly right-skewed, over 50% of scholars are associated with negative signed marginal effects on the journal-period average. These values should not be interpreted as penalties or judgments of scholarly quality; rather, they are a structural inevitability of average-based indicators and reflect the mechanical behavior when publication-level citation rates fall below the relevant journal mean. By relaxing the monotonicity constraint, this study aligns attribution models with the mathematical reality of scholarly metrics, providing a nuanced understanding of how individual output shapes collective performance indicators.

title: On association between the research performance of academic advisors and their PhD students
abstract: Abstract In this paper, we examine whether and how the research performance of advisors is associated with that of their PhD students. We analyze the entire population of PhD students in Slovenia who successfully defended their theses, along with their advisors, between 1988 and 2022. For each individual, we compute five bibliometric indicators (covering the publication activities, collaboration patterns, and research independence) within a five-year interval around the PhD defense and use these values to classify students and advisors into six performance classes. Our results show that while students mirror their advisors’ collaboration patterns, their productivity and independence exhibit weak and negative correlations, respectively, although significant differences are observed across scientific disciplines. Additionally, over the past 35 years, student–advisor dynamics have generally shifted from independent relationships to more collaborative ones. Today’s students are more integrated into their advisors’ research networks and have more coauthors, while their productivity shows a downward trend. Our findings highlight the uneven distribution of mentorship effects and suggest practical implications for doctoral programs, including the need to strengthen support mechanisms that help students to select suitable advisors.

title: Ptsl: a semantic structure-based patent transfer path prediction model using large language models and heterogeneous network analysis
abstract: Patent technology transfer is the core driving force of technological progress. Precise prediction of patent transfer paths plays an essential role in enhancing technology transfer efficiency. However, existing methods lack modeling of fine-grained semantic structural relationships in patent subject texts, and lack in-depth mining of homogeneous and heterogeneous relationships in complex patent networks. Therefore, we propose a Patent Transfer path prediction based on the Semantic structure of patent text topics for Large language models (PTSL). First, we design an Adaptive Weighted Intra-class and Inter-class relationship modeling for a specific heterogeneous patent network (AWII). Through a double-layer attention mechanism, we adaptively learn the association weights of patents in the same field in the intra-class dimension and capture the semantic mapping strength of cross-field patents in the inter-class dimension, thereby achieving hierarchical modeling of multivariate relationships in heterogeneous networks. Secondly, we design a Semantic Fine-grained modeling strategy that combines Large Language Models and BERT contextual representation (SF-LLM). SF-LLM’s deep semantic understanding ability is used to parse the subject structure of long text patents and generate a fine-grained patent technology roadmap expansion diagram containing technical concepts, associations, and semantic levels. Additionally, we introduce BERT to generate patent subject representations and adopted a contextual attention mechanism to achieve contextual semantic enhancement of patent representations. Third, we design a patent Semantic extension graph and heterogeneous patent Representation Enhancement Framework (SREF), which uses LLM-generated semantic extension graph embeddings as enhancement constraints, re-encodes heterogeneous patent embeddings, and regenerates based on patent subject semantics, thus achieving dynamic coupling between patent technology subject semantic representations and network structural features. Finally, we empirically evaluate the PTSL model on cross-domain patent transfer path datasets. Comparative experiments show our method outperforms baselines by 5.78% in accuracy, 1.47% in precision, 8.15% in recall, and 4.81% in F1-score, verifying that the PTSL model not only enhances patent transfer path prediction accuracy but also provides an intelligent and reliable tool for university-enterprise patent technology transfer.

title: Modeling for the claims clarity of chinese patents: based on multi-level linguistic feature extraction
abstract: The clarity of patent claims is fundamental to defining the scope of legal protection, yet large-scale assessment remains methodologically challenging, especially in non-English patent systems. To address this gap, we develop a machine-learning framework that evaluates the clarity of Chinese patent claims by extracting multi-level linguistic features from the lexical, syntactic, and discourse-related dimensions of patent texts. Trained on reexamination decisions under Article 26(4) of the Chinese Patent Law and supervised with continuous scores derived from reexamination outcomes (rather than binary clear/unclear labels) to reflect varying degrees of linguistic ambiguity, the framework models claims clarity as a continuous rather than binary attribute. The best-performing specification, based on support vector regression (SVR), exhibits strong predictive performance and robustness. Its validity is further supported by alternative sampling strategies and external validation using award-winning patent data. The validated model is then applied to 127,475 granted patents in China’s strategic emerging industries. The results show that clarity decreases with vague expressions, redundant wording, and overly lengthy claim texts. Conversely, clarity improves when claims employ precise qualifiers, exhibit cohesive syntactic connections, and maintain strong terminological and logical alignment with the specification (i.e., claims–specification coherence). Claims clarity also varies systematically across applicant types and industry sectors. Patents filed by universities and individual applicants, as well as patents in new materials and high-end equipment manufacturing, exhibit higher clarity than corporate patents and patents in information technology or biomedicine. Further analyses suggest that greater claims clarity is associated with faster and broader technological diffusion, as reflected in shorter citation delays and larger IPC-based technological differences, and with a higher likelihood of patent transactions. These findings indicate that linguistic transparency in patent claims may be linked to both the informational effectiveness of patent disclosure and the marketability of patented knowledge. More broadly, the study provides a scalable approach to measuring claims clarity in a non-English patent system and offers empirical evidence on how patent information quality is associated with innovation diffusion and technology-market outcomes.

title: Toward responsible scientometrics: a lifecycle framework of normative data practices for research evaluation
abstract: Responsible scientometrics has become a central concern in the context of increasing reliance on bibliometric indicators for research evaluation and policy decision-making. While existing frameworks such as DORA, the Leiden Manifesto, and CoARA emphasize principles of responsible metrics, less attention has been paid to the underlying data practices that condition the validity, transparency, and reproducibility of scientometric studies. This paper argues that responsible scientometrics cannot be achieved solely through improved indicators or evaluation principles; it also depends critically on the normative structuring of data practices across the entire research lifecycle. We propose a lifecycle-based framework that conceptualizes scientometric research as a sequence of interdependent data practices, including data source selection, data retrieval and acquisition, data preprocessing and standardization, data analysis and visualization, data interpretation, data storage and documentation, and data sharing and citation. For each stage, we identify common methodological risks and propose normative guidelines aimed at improving transparency, reproducibility, and contextual validity. By integrating methodological considerations with principles of responsible research assessment, the framework highlights how data practices are not merely technical procedures but constitutive elements of evaluation outcomes. The proposed framework contributes to scientometrics in three ways: (1) it systematizes scattered methodological recommendations into a coherent lifecycle model; (2) it extends responsible metrics discussions by foregrounding data-level normativity; and (3) it provides a practical reference for researchers, reviewers, and policy stakeholders engaged in research evaluation. Ultimately, this work aims to strengthen the methodological foundations of scientometrics and support more transparent, accountable, and context-sensitive evaluation systems.

title: Publication productivity and citation visibility in Turkish gastronomy and culinary arts: a population-level scientometric analysis of academic staff, 2020–2024
abstract: This study provides a population-level scientometric analysis of indexed publication productivity, citation-based visibility, thematic structure, and collaboration patterns in Gastronomy and Culinary Arts (GCA) in Türkiye. Using a near-census dataset of 412 academics across 95 GCA departments, the study examines publication outputs produced between 2020 and 2024 through negative binomial regression, principal component analysis, and bibliometric network mapping. The findings show that cumulative advantage operates selectively within Turkish GCA. Academic rank is more strongly associated with accumulated visibility indicators, such as citations and h-index, than with recent indexed publication volume. Recent output is instead more closely associated with career-stage dynamics and university governance type, with academics in public universities publishing at higher rates than those in foundation universities. Institutional age and provincial socio-economic development show limited independent explanatory power after individual and institutional factors are considered. Network analysis reveals a dual thematic structure, combining a gastronomy–tourism core with a food science-oriented strand connected through sustainability, food safety, and applied research themes. International collaboration is present but selective, with stronger links concentrated around European partners. The study contributes to scientometric scholarship by showing how output accumulation and citation-based visibility may follow different patterns within Turkish GCA. Findings are interpreted within the boundaries of Turkish GCA, and comparative research is needed to assess their broader applicability.

title: Productivity rate metrics for awards and investigators funded by the US National Cancer Institute
abstract: Abstract The proposed scholarly and societal metrics reflect the output efficiency of extramural research funded by the US National Cancer Institute. The productivity of awards or investigators (AoIs) expressed as output COst INdexes (COINs) were calculated based on AoI-linked qualified research articles (qRA) published in single years that follow the AoI-funded years. The outputs for qualified years manifested as either qRA counts or sums of qRA-specific impact values were normalized by the total multi-year amount of funding and, for fractional metrics, by the number of the qRA funders and co-authors. Calculations of the basic (overall) COINs (B-COINs) included all qRAs while translational COINs (T-COINs) were based on a subset of qRAs cited by clinical practice guidelines published by major professional cancer associations. Higher B-COIN values were associated with Early Stage Investigator (ESI) group as compared to non-ESIs. The Outstanding Investigator designation correlated with B-COIN decrease. In multi-component grants, higher B-COINs were observed for the Specialized Programs of Research Excellence (SPORE) project co-leaders (PCLs) funded by SPOREs as compared to performance of the same investigators serving as Principal Investigators (PIs) of other research awards. In contrast, performance of the Program Project Grant (P01) subproject PIs was invariable regardless of the funding source and lower than that of SPORE PCLs supported by SPOREs. The highest T-COINs were associated with awards supporting late phase clinical trials, intermediate values noted for programs focused on early translation (SPOREs), followed by P01 and Research Project Grants (R01). Statistical evidence linked to performance-based metrics may facilitate more efficient investment policies at grant-funding institutions.

title: Evaluating the reliability of web of science citation function classification: evidence from manual annotation and large language models
abstract: The Web of Science (WoS) recently introduced citation function classification to identify the roles that cited references play within scientific texts. As these labels may increasingly be used for retrieval and evaluative analyses, their reliability warrants systematic assessment. Focusing on the “Basis” category—arguably the most substantively interpretable citation function—we evaluate WoS classifications against a manually annotated gold standard and large language models (LLMs) predictions. Using 3,318 citation sentences extracted from PLOS articles on COVID-19, we compare WoS labels with human annotations and LLM-based classifications. Results show that while WoS exhibits high precision in identifying Basis citations, it systematically under-detects them, with the majority of errors attributable to false negatives rather than false positives. Error analysis reveals that implicit methodological usage, proper noun references, and contextual inference requirements contribute substantially to these omissions. In contrast, LLM-based models achieve higher overall accuracy and substantially reduce missed cases, though they require enhanced sensitivity to sentence-level citation markers. These findings suggest that WoS citation function labels should be used cautiously in recall-sensitive analyses. More broadly, this study demonstrates how LLM-based annotation can serve as an auditing tool for database-level algorithmic classifications and provides empirical insights into the transition from rule-based to semantic citation function classification.

title: Comparing for the best: reinforcement learning for source citation identification with large language models
abstract: Although research papers typically contain many citations, not all of them contribute equally to the core ideas or methodological foundations of the paper. Source citation identification (SCI) aims to identify, for a query paper, the cited papers that contribute the core ideas or foundational methodologies from among all its references. This problem plays a crucial role in advancing science and technology, enabling a wide range of applications such as scientific evolution analysis, citation recommendation, and influence prediction. However, SCI remains challenging for two main reasons. First, source citations are sparse, and this sparsity makes it difficult to design effective mechanisms for comparing and evaluating candidate citations. Second, academic papers typically contain long textual content, making it challenging to fully capture and leverage global contextual information. To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel framework, named ReSCILLMs ( Re inforcement learning for S ource C itation I dentification with L arge L anguage M odel s ). Within the reinforcement learning paradigm, SCI is reformulated as a sequential decision-making problem rather than a conventional classification task. The framework leverages the deep textual representations provided by large language models (LLMs). To further mitigate the sparse reward issue, a carefully designed graph-based reward mechanism is introduced. ReSCILLMs is tailored to be compatible with various open-source LLMs, and is optimized using the proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm. Extensive experiments have been conducted within the environment built on the OAG-PST dataset, employing open-source LLMs including SciBERT, Gemma, and Llama. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed models significantly outperform baseline approaches in terms of success rate with improvements ranging from approximately 3% to 16%, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of success rate.

title: Growth, concentration, and internationalisation of research output at a post-reform regional university in Ecuador: bibliometric evidence from Scopus (2016–2025)
abstract: Bibliometric analyses of research output at the level of a single institution are rare for emerging regional universities in the Global South. This situation creates gaps in the evidence available to accreditation bodies and institutional decision-makers who operate within active higher education reform frameworks. The present study offers a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of Scopus-indexed publications affiliated with the Universidad Técnica de Manabí (UTM) in Ecuador over a decade. It covers five analytical dimensions: growth trajectory, thematic diversification, workforce productivity and citation concentration, co-authorship network formation, and publication quality. A programmatic Python pipeline, developed with Scopus APIs, collected, deduplicated, and enriched a corpus of documents. Bibliometric indicators included compound annual growth rates, the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, Gini coefficients and Lorenz curves, Louvain community detection, and SJR quartile profiling. The output of the university expanded dramatically over the decade, following a two-phase pattern of explosive growth followed by consolidation. No discernible disruption occurred due to a major earthquake or the COVID-19 pandemic. Disciplinary coverage broadened from one active subject area to several others. The co-authorship network transitioned from fragmentation to near-full connectivity. The share of high-quality journal articles increased substantially by the end. Two structural vulnerabilities emerged: severe citation concentration, with a small number of researchers accounting for a large portion of institutional impact, and open access availability dominated by publisher-controlled models. The findings demonstrate how higher education reform policy can drive rapid and sustained research capacity building at a peripheral university, while also generating structural asymmetries that require deliberate institutional strategies to address.

title: How robust are Weibo altmetrics data? A first exploration
abstract: This study aims to evaluate the robustness of Weibo Altmetrics data, providing insights into the usefulness of this important local altmetrics data source for scholarly dissemination and evaluation. All Weibo altmetrics data indexed in the Altmetric database were harvested. A ten-year time window was used to observe the difference. The robustness was investigated using a hybrid framework combining temporal analysis, dissemination structure and users’ perspective, to shed light on the temporal stability and influencing factors of Weibo altmetrics data. Findings indicate that: (1) Approximately 32.07% of Weibo mentions were inaccessible. (2) The primary reason for inaccessibility was post-deletion, followed by automatic expiration due to Weibo’s visibility time limits. (3) Newer publications exhibited higher mention accessibility rates. (4) Higher originality and higher concentration of academic papers correlated with lower mention inaccessibility rates. (5) User behavior significantly impacted post survival. These findings offer empirical support for long-term impact assessments using Weibo altmetrics.

title: European doctoral dissertations in education from 1701 to 1900: a scientometric approach to their origins
abstract: In this study, we conducted a scientometric review of European doctoral dissertations in the field of education defended between 1701 and 1900. The topic addressed is multidisciplinary in nature, integrating scientometric, historical, geopolitical, and educational dimensions, and entails a singular level of complexity. Variables were defined in relation to thematic areas; descriptors provided by databases and inferred from dissertation titles; year of defense; language, and the universities, faculties, and countries where the dissertations were defended, as well as two additional formal variables: publisher identity and dissertation length, measured in pages. In conclusion, the field of European doctoral dissertations in education defended throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries reveals notable thematic richness, diversity of topics, and alignment with established scientometric patterns. Already at that time, the tension between generalist and specialist disciplines appears as a consolidated characteristic, reflecting a field that, from its inception, oscillated between theoretical synthesis and disciplinary specialization. At the same time, the Franco-German axis becomes visible as a seminal driver of the growth of European dissertations in education, fostering dynamics that laid the foundations for the consolidation of education as a modern, multidisciplinary field.

title: Co-opetition network structures and multidimensional research impact among higher education institutions: evidence from a two-layer relational network and community-based analysis
abstract: Higher education institutions operate within a dynamic framework of co-opetition, simultaneously collaborating in activities such as joint research while competing for resources, reputation, and recognition. This interplay is closely related to the production, dissemination, and broader transformation of scientific knowledge. Examining how co-opetition network structures are associated with the academic and societal impact of institutional research can provide useful insights for higher education governance and science policy design. Using submission and evaluation outcome data from REF2021, this study constructs separate competition and cooperation networks among 155 UK higher education institutions and integrates them into a multilayer network. The multilayer Infomap algorithm is then applied to detect institutional communities, from which community-level structural features are extracted as indicators of the co-opetition network environment. The study further examines how these network structures are associated with institutional academic and societal impact. The empirical findings show that institutions’ research environment quality and the degree of cooperative imbalance are significantly and positively associated with both academic and societal impact. Mean competitive strength is positively associated with academic impact, whereas competitive imbalance is negatively associated with academic impact. By contrast, community size shows a significant positive association with societal impact. These findings suggest that academic and societal impact are related to different co-opetition network mechanisms: academic impact is more closely associated with competitive intensity and balance within academic communities, while societal impact is more strongly linked to the breadth of community-based knowledge diffusion.

title: Libraries, research and development funding, and economic prosperity: data for the holistic university
abstract: Abstract Macro indicators of Research and Development (R&D) such as numbers of journal publications and citation rates, patents, impact factors, and R&D expenditures have become proxies for economic competitiveness. But quantifying relationships between macro-indicators and budgets supporting these indirect metrics of R&D are sparse, and some factors critical to the holistic university, such as expenditures on libraries, have been missed. We quantified post-1945 relationships between federal research and development (R&D) funding to large universities and individual university rankings and regional economic prosperity in the United States. Empirical data, substantiated by a principal component analysis of multiple additional university-specific factors, reveals that there are $21.34 of R&D expenditures for each $1 of library expenditures at 71 public universities; arts and humanities programs are a positive influence for acquiring R&D funds. University rankings for > 90 universities are also positively correlated to R&D expenditures. There is a $1:$264 ratio of state-wide R&D expenditures to state’s gross economic production ( R 2 = 0.86), and a $1:$59 ratio for a state’s per capita R&D expenditure vs. per capita income ( R 2 = 0.34). These empirical relationships can guide budget decisions. They support the conclusion that effective university R&D is fostered by a holistic framework espousing scholarship through research, teaching, and public service benefiting state-scale populations, and are currently at risk.

title: Scientific mobility, prestige and topic alignment in research institutions
abstract: Abstract Research institutions are crucial in driving intellectual, social, and technological progress. Their ability to innovate depends mainly on their ability to attract, retain, and nurture scientific talent, ultimately making it available to other organizations, industries, or the economy. As researchers change institutions during their careers, their research topics also shift. The extent and mechanisms by which research institutions manage their internal portfolio of scientific topics through the attraction and deployment of researchers are far from well understood. We examine 25 million publication histories of 9.2 million scientists extracted from a large-scale bibliographic database covering thousands of research institutions worldwide to understand how the topics of mobile scientists align with those present in-house. We find a correlation between top-ranked institutions and greater topic alignment, i.e., the degree to which topics of incoming academics match those of their colleagues at the institution. We uncover a similarly high level of alignment among scientists leaving top-ranked institutions. The alignment of research topics in research institutions is more pronounced in engineering, life, health, earth, and physical sciences than in mathematics, computer science, social sciences, and the humanities. We show that institutions have generally become more closely aligned in their overall topic profile over the past two decades. We interpret these results in terms of the levels of proactive management of the composition of the scientific workforce and internal collaboration strategies at the institutional level.

title: Exploring the Too-Much-Talent effect in academic fields: Evidence from the National Institutes of Health in the United States
abstract: This study investigates the Too-Much-Talent (TMT) effect, a phenomenon where additional top talents enhance team performance up to a certain point, beyond which the advantages diminish and may lead to negative outcomes, by analyzing bibliographic data and applying various statistical methods across the National Institutes of Health (NIH) institutes and centers (ICs). We analyzed bibliographic data from 56,400 articles published by NIH ICs between 2011 and 2020. Regression analyses were conducted using six functions (linear, quadratic, cubic, log, logistic, and power) and piecewise linear regression to examine the relationship between the proportion of top-talented researchers and team performance. The log function generally provided a better fit than the quadratic function across NIH ICs. At most one IC showed evidence of a TMT effect, and this effect was not statistically robust. However, employing alternative methods to assess top talent and team performance may produce different results. We expect our findings to serve as a valuable foundation for policymakers organizing or managing research teams.

title: The impact of changing metrics in Shanghai Ranking’s Global Ranking of Academic Subjects on medical sciences subjects
abstract: Abstract This article examines the longitudinal stability, internal consistency, and stratifying effects of Shanghai Ranking’s Global Ranking of Academic Subjects (Shanghai GRAS) in six subjects of Medical Sciences (2017–2025). While Shanghai GRAS has gained prominence as a global higher education benchmark, little is known about the empirical consequences of its methodological changes. Using a quantitative approach combining descriptive statistics, indicator score and overall score change analysis, and K-means clustering, we evaluated the effects of indicator revisions, weight adjustments, and new data sources on institutional trajectories. Our findings show that global methodological alterations influencing all subjects generate substantial volatility, especially for institutions outside the top clusters. The 2019 Category Normalized Citation Impact revision corresponded with overall score increases, while the 2024 methodology restructuring led to significant score declines in general, but the rankings of leading institutions either improved or were not affected. Our findings challenge assumptions about the comparability of rankings and reveal their performative role in reinforcing institutional hierarchies, while also calling for more transparent, context-sensitive evaluation frameworks that reflect the epistemic diversity of global academia.

title: Pink queue and double standard: new evidence on gender gaps from the Italian academia
abstract: Abstract Gender disparities in academic careers remain pronounced, particularly in access to the highest ranks. This paper provides new evidence on these inequalities by modeling academic career progression as a dynamic process. Using a Markov multi-state model, we analyze transitions across academic ranks for the entire population of professors employed in Italian universities between 2016 and 2021. This approach allows us to estimate not only promotion probabilities, but also the expected time required to reach Full professorship. We find that women reach promotion with lower probability and in more years than men, even after accounting for their scientific research output, seniority, and willingness to compete. Although gender gaps narrow when considering an entire career horizon, they never disappear. Importantly, we document that women with a given level of research performance display promotion probabilities systematically similar to those of men with lower research performance, suggesting unequal returns to merit, mirroring other double standards observed in other sectors of the labor market. Our analysis also shows that for women it takes systematically more time to get promotion, a result labeled as pink queue. This study contributes both substantively, by providing a comprehensive assessment of gender disparities in academia, and methodologically, by demonstrating the value of dynamic multi-state models to enrich the study of career progression in structured labor markets.

title: The field-weighted citation impact metric does not adequately account for publication age
abstract: Abstract To investigate the association between publication month and field-weighted citation impact (FWCI), a cross-sectional study was conducted using 2.1 million medical publications from SciVal, from the 10 countries with the most publications, during 2019–2023. Publications from January and December were excluded due to inaccurate recording of publication dates in SciVal. Quantile regression was used to estimate the association between publication month and FWCI quantiles (50th, 75th, 95th, and 99th percentiles) for 2019–2023 and each separate year. Median FWCI decreased, on average, by 0.030 per month (95% CI: 0.029, 0.031). The equivalent FWCI decreases for the 75th, 95th, and 99th percentiles were 0.067 (95% CI: 0.066, 0.068), 0.232 (95% CI: 0.227, 0.237), and 0.580 (95% CI: 0.553, 0.607), respectively. The median FWCI in November (0.46) was 39% less than the median FWCI in February (0.75). The strength of association between publication month and FWCI percentile was stronger for more recent publication years. When using data for 2023, the median FWCI decreased, on average, by 0.065 per month (95% CI: 0.064, 0.066), compared to 0.017 per month (95% CI: 0.016, 0.018) when using data from 2019. The median FWCI in November 2023 was 64% less than the median FWCI in February 2023, compared to 28% for the equivalent difference in 2019. These findings demonstrate a strong association between FWCI and the month of publication. FWCI is a biased indicator of research impact and needs to account for publication-age dependence by comparing articles from the same month, not only the same year.

title: Research on joint classification of interdisciplinary term mention motivation-sentiment and fusion measurement based on large language models
abstract: Interdisciplinary term usage encodes both citing purposes and evaluative attitudes, serving as an important lens for understanding knowledge interaction across disciplines. However, existing approaches typically model term mention motivation (TMM) and term mention sentiment (TMS) as independent tasks, neglecting their semantic interdependence at the term level and limiting fine-grained analysis of interdisciplinary knowledge integration. To address this gap, a prompt-based LLM joint classification framework is developed to integrate TMM classification (TMMC) and TMS classification (TMSC), together with a multi-dimensional fusion measurement that combines the Interdisciplinary Impact Index (III), Structural Distribution Index (SDI), and Normalized Diversity Index (NDI). Using a dataset of 20,042 interdisciplinary terms spanning 23 citing disciplines, TMM is categorized into explanatory, applied, and non-functional mentions, while TMS is classified as positive, neutral, and negative. The results show that simultaneous prediction of TMM and TMS achieves competitive performance across tasks, with GLM4-9B achieving the best performance (weighted F1-scores of 83.52% for TMMC and 79.97% for TMSC). The proposed fusion measurement further enables effective differentiation of terms with varying levels of interdisciplinary integration. These findings provide a scalable and fine-grained analytical framework for interdisciplinary knowledge analysis, offering methodological support for understanding knowledge integration patterns and evaluating interdisciplinary research.

title: Responds to Nazarovets’: poor bibliometric studies do not make bibliometrics poor science: a response to Ellegaard
Bibliometric performance and uncertainty in heterogeneous research groups: trends in authorship and fractional citation indicators
abstract: Abstract Bibliometric indicators are widely used to evaluate scientific performance, despite well-known limitations related to disciplinary differences, collaboration practices, and strategic responses to evaluation systems. Traditional metrics such as the H-index are particularly sensitive to the number of co-authors and to the length of reference lists, both of which have exhibited strong historical growth. This study analyzes the temporal evolution of authorship, referencing, and productivity patterns in six research populations (four Italian Scientific Disciplinary Sectors in engineering and two international conference communities), covering 1,286 researchers and 86,351 publications. The results reveal systematic increases in authors per article, references per article, and documents per author, with structural changes that coincide with technological developments and the introduction of bibliometric criteria in national evaluation policies. Building on fractional counting, we propose a new citation-based indicator in which publication credit is shared among co-authors and each incoming citation is weighted by the inverse of the number of references in the citing article. Comparisons with the H-index show strong overall correlations, but indicate that the proposed indicator attenuates the advantage associated with hyper-authorship and inflated reference lists and reduces variability across heterogeneous research groups. Adopting a measurement-theoretic perspective, we further assess the uncertainty of bibliometric indicators by analyzing linear trends with researcher seniority and the dispersion of individual data around these trends. The proposed indicator exhibits a slightly more homogeneous trend across heterogeneous research groups and shows strong overall correlation with the H-index, suggesting that it may provide a more comparable representation of scientific performance across diverse research communities.

title: Implementing relational goods for responsible research evaluation
abstract: Responsible research evaluation requires methods capable of recognising not only research outputs but also the relational practices through which scientific knowledge is generated. This contribution proposes an operational framework for incorporating relational goods into research evaluation by integrating bibliometric, administrative, narrative, AI-assisted and qualitative sources of evidence. The framework identifies eight relational domains, specifies their associated relational and internal goods, and links them to potential indicators and complementary data sources. It also distinguishes between relational dimensions that can be informed by existing evidence and those that require additional qualitative evidence, such as structured interviews or questionnaires. An illustrative empirical application shows the feasibility of the proposed approach.

title: Large language models for literature-based analysis: constructing ontology-grounded citation knowledge graphs
abstract: Abstract This work introduces a novel framework to construct ontology grounded knowledge graphs using contexts from citation sentiment dataset and incorporating large language models LLMs for literature grounded analysis. Recent studies look at the perspectives of ontologies, citation intent and information extraction separately, this work combines these concepts in a single end to end pipeline. The proposed framework uses a small locally hosted LLM along with a subset of the Citation Typing Ontology (CiTO) to decide which relation to assign, applies filtering based on confidence score, finds out the smallest supporting evidence span and finally creates a knowledge graph. In the knowledge graph the relation, intent, stance and evidence of each citation example is stored, and each example is treated as a separate instance. The experiments report results on the SciCite dataset and show that the pipeline finds out smaller evidence spans than the full context for most of the examples, a significant part of data is preserved after the confidence based filtering and most of the assertions are kept. To summarize, this paper addresses the challenges of entity extraction and semantic reasoning and shows that citation contexts can be converted into auditable knowledge graphs backed by confidence score.

title: From paper content to journal quality: an LLM-based comparative assessment approach within the REF 2021 framework
abstract: Previous research has shown that large language model (LLM)-based assessments of individual articles can be aggregated into journal-level indicators. This study further compares two forms of LLM output generated within the same REF-guided pairwise assessment task and examines their relative performance in journal evaluation. Using UK REF 2021 submissions in UoA 5 (Biological Sciences), we construct a dataset linking journal articles to departmental REF quality profiles, citation indicators, and cleaned English abstracts. An LLM is configured as a “virtual REF reviewer” to compare pairs of papers using only their titles and abstracts, producing both REF-style 1*–4* ratings and binary preferences. From these outputs, we derive two LLM-based journal indicators: LLM_REF, based on aggregated REF-style ratings, and BT_score, based on binary preferences aggregated through Bradley–Terry estimation. These indicators are benchmarked against a REF-derived departmental proxy (Dept REF mean) and citation-based indicators (MNLCS and SJR). The results show that LLM_REF achieves higher agreement with the journal tier classifications generated by Dept REF mean than BT_score. Correlation analysis further shows that LLM_REF has stronger rank correlations with Dept REF mean than BT_score, with the relationship between LLM_REF and Dept REF mean becoming stronger when journals are represented by more papers. These findings show that, in the REF 2021 UoA 5 setting, REF-style ratings perform better than binary preferences for journal evaluation when both are generated within the same LLM-based pairwise comparison task.

title: Research productivity and funding efficiency in Spain: a bibliometric analysis of the national R&D plan (2018–2020)
abstract: This study analyzes the productivity and funding efficiency of research projects funded under the Spanish National R&D Plan (2018–2020) using a bibliometric approach. Two datasets were integrated: 5309 funded projects and 44,646 articles indexed in Web of Science linked to these projects. Indicators of productivity (articles per project), efficiency (cost per article), and concentration (Pareto curves) were calculated at both the subfield and disciplinary area levels. The results reveal substantial disciplinary heterogeneity. Subfields such as Mathematics, Chemistry, Astronomy and Astrophysics, Computer Science, and Nuclear and Particle Physics exhibit high productivity levels and relatively low costs per article, whereas disciplines such as Law, Arts, and Language and Literature show very low publication outputs and high unit costs. The concentration analysis highlights a markedly asymmetric pattern: 50% of the articles are concentrated in only 13.8% of the projects, and the top 20% of projects account for around 61% of total scientific output. These findings underscore the risks of applying uniform bibliometric indicators in the evaluation of research projects, as they systematically disadvantage disciplines with distinct patterns of scientific communication. They also highlight the need to move towards a more equitable and discipline-sensitive funding system in Spain, combining bibliometric indicators with qualitative metrics and measures of social impact.

title: Exploring the patterns of citation-related static features of highly cited papers across disciplines
abstract: Although numerous studies have examined paper characteristics associated with overall citation impact, limited attention has been paid to how differences in these characteristics evolve across successive levels of citation impact. This study addresses this gap by examining the hierarchical and disciplinary patterns of multidimensional citation-related static features (CRSFs). Leveraging Web of Science articles and reviews published from 2009 to 2021 in Physics ( N = 1,299,999), Social Sciences General ( N = 983,742), and Environment/Ecology ( N = 634,297), papers were classified into six percentile rank (PR) classes based on citation counts. A Propensity Score Matching (PSM) approach was employed to improve the comparability of papers in adjacent PR classes by controlling potential confounding effects before comparing each target feature, while effect size analysis was used to quantify the practical magnitude of these differences. Results reveal substantial disciplinary heterogeneity in the association between paper length and citation impact. The relationship is positive in Physics but negative in Social Sciences General and Environment/Ecology. Effect size analyses indicate that reference-related features are the very important CRSFs dimension, but dominant indicators vary across disciplines. As citation-impact level increases, CRSFs differences generally diminish, but the gap widens markedly between the top 1% papers and those in the top 1%–5% class, suggesting that top-tier highly cited papers are not simply a linear extension of other highly cited papers. The practical effects of the number of authors, the number of institutions, and paper length are relatively limited among highly cited papers. Overall, this study uncovers hierarchical and disciplinary heterogeneity in CRSFs-citation impact relationships, providing new insights into the characteristics associated with highly cited papers.

title: Mapping the evolution of artificial intelligence: an LLM-driven patent network analysis
abstract: Traditional patent analysis methods, which often rely on International Patent Classification codes or keyword co-occurrence, have limited ability to recover the hierarchical relations embedded in complex technological systems. To address this limitation, this study develops an LLM-assisted bibliometric framework to extract minimal functional units and organize them into parent–child technical structures from patent texts. Applying this framework to 774,737 global artificial intelligence patent records with application dates from 2000 to 2024, we construct a time-varying semantic technology network. Using community detection, PageRank, and normalized mutual information, we examine how the internal structure of AI technologies changes over time. The results suggest a nonlinear evolutionary trajectory in which AI shifted from relatively dispersed algorithmic configurations toward more modular and hierarchically organized architectures in which data-processing, representation, and model-training-related components became more visible. Changes in PageRank and eigenvector centrality indicate shifts in the structural prominence of data-handling, representation, and model-training-related components. Overall, the study shows how LLM-based structural extraction can complement existing scientometric approaches by providing a component-level view of technological change.

title: Research quality metrics as a complement to bibliometrics: an opinion paper
abstract: Abstract Substantial proportions of research investment may be wasted due to flawed study design, biased reporting, and publication bias, raising concerns about how research performance is evaluated. Despite this, current assessment systems rely heavily on bibliometric indicators such as publication counts, co-authorship, and citation metrics, which do not reliably reflect research quality or scientific rigor. In this opinion paper, we argue that such indicators may reward practices that undermine the accumulation of reliable knowledge, including p-hacking, selective reporting, and underpowered study designs, while undervaluing essential contributions such as replication research. We propose that bibliometric measures should be complemented by transparent and auditable research quality metrics, including indicators of reproducibility, statistical power, risk of bias, and adherence to reporting standards. We further suggest that recent advances in large language models may facilitate the scalable implementation of such metrics. Adopting quality-focused indicators could improve research evaluation and help reduce avoidable research waste.

title: Identifying and evaluating emerging scientific trends through temporal n-gram analysis
abstract: Abstract The rapid growth of scientific publishing creates both opportunities and challenges for understanding emerging research trends. Traditional approaches to trend detection, such as citation analyses or latent topic models, often lag behind real developments or lack interpretability. To address these limitations, this study proposes a lightweight and transparent methodology for detecting and evaluating emerging scientific concepts through temporal n -gram analysis. From the OpenAlex corpus of scholarly metadata, n -grams are extracted from titles and abstracts, and aggregated into quarterly frequency series. Bursty dynamics are identified using complementary detection algorithms, including Kleinberg’s state-machine model and a moving average convergence divergence (MACD) approach. Evaluation uses a human-centered framework in which participants judge temporal plots of anonymized n -grams, providing both pairwise comparisons and graded burstiness scores. These judgments are compared with algorithmic rankings, and alignment between large language models (LLMs) and human raters is examined. We further contrast burst dynamics across fast- and slow-evolving subfields and verify the robustness of the approach to corpus-growth effects through a normalization experiment. By integrating scalable temporal analysis and multi-perspective evaluation, this work contributes a framework for monitoring and characterizing the trajectory of emerging research topics. The approach is intended as an interpretable tool for digital libraries, funding agencies, and research analysts seeking to navigate fast-evolving scientific landscapes.

title: High correlation, unstable rankings: profile-dependent disagreement between career-based and single-year bibliometric evaluation
abstract: Bibliometric indicators capture different temporal dimensions of scientific achievement, but strong correlation between them does not necessarily imply stable individual-level ranking. Here, I compared career-based and single-year-based standings within the same researchers in a matched Biology sample from the 2024 edition of the Top 2% Scientist dataset. I defined the excellence gap as the single-year percentile minus the career-based percentile and evaluated high standing directly through membership in top-cut sets under the two evaluation windows. The two rank-derived percentile measures showed substantial aggregate correspondence (Pearson correlation between the rank-derived percentiles, r = 0.698), yet individual standings were frequently reordered: the median absolute excellence gap was 0.129 on the 0–1 percentile scale, equivalent to 12.9 percentile points, and 58.6% of researchers had an absolute gap of at least 0.10, or 10 percentile points. Multivariable analyses showed that these discrepancies were systematically associated with career length, productivity density, and authorship-citation profiles. Shorter, high-intensity publication histories were associated with relatively higher single-year standing, whereas longer and more cumulative profiles were associated with relatively higher career-based standing. In the primary field-adjusted analytic subset, high standing overlapped substantially but incompletely: 66.8% of researchers in the career-based top quintile were also in the single-year top quintile, the reverse retention was 67.1%, and the Jaccard overlap was 0.503. Descriptive clustering provided a resampling-stable summary of profile heterogeneity, although much of the apparent cluster-level variation in the excellence gap was attenuated after adjustment for continuous covariates. These findings indicate that strong aggregate agreement between bibliometric indicators does not imply interchangeability in individual-level evaluation. Metric choice should therefore be reported transparently and interpreted as one dimension of assessment rather than as a neutral or universal ranking of scientific performance.

title: Technology scanning: a systematic mapping review using text analytics
abstract: Abstract In rapidly changing technological environments, companies must effectively identify and evaluate technological changes to sustain their dynamic capabilities. The growing body of research on technology scanning and innovation trajectories makes it difficult to perform systematic literature reviews using traditional methods alone. Many existing reviews rely on citation-based indicators or manual screening procedures, which can limit scalability and make it difficult to capture the evolving structure of the literature. This paper presents a text-analytics systematic mapping review of the technology-scanning literature. The workflow combines corpus construction, machine-learning–based screening, topic modeling, clustering, and similarity-based mapping to support the systematic analysis of research on technology scanning and technological change detection. Using a large collection of publications retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus, the workflow presented in this paper identifies methodological approaches, thematic structure, and emerging analytical trends in the technology scanning literature, including human-in-the-loop topic modeling, semi-supervised and guided topic modeling, and reinforcement learning-based approaches. The resulting topic clusters and their associated documents are analyzed and mapped to three main research questions (A, B, and C) and eleven corresponding sub-questions presented in Table 2. The results show that existing studies are rich in concepts but fragmented, with most models relying on predefined variables and lacking adaptive mechanisms to capture technological change. Several approaches are also semi-automated and rely on human interpretation. Even recent AI-driven approaches that generate analytical outputs are not connected to transparent analytical workflows and do not support continuous knowledge updates. The proposed workflow demonstrates how topic modeling and similarity-based analysis can be incorporated into a systematic mapping review of technology-scanning research. The findings highlight opportunities for developing more adaptive and continuously updated approaches to technology scanning.

title: Research on technology evolution analysis method from the problem–solution-effect (PSE) three-dimensional perspective
abstract: Abstract Technological evolution analysis is critical to identify technology opportunities and develop innovation strategy. Existing approaches represent patents as keywords, topics or syntactic triples, overlooking the causality of the inventive process. This paper introduces a PSE (Problem–Solution-Effect) framework that considers technology evolution as the dynamics of technical problem elements, solution elements and effect elements. To operate the PSE framework, we propose a PSE-based approach for technological evolution analysis, by identifying the PSE elements through Topic Model from related patent sentences extracted by large language models, constructing the PSE heterogeneous network based on co-occurrence relation among PSE elements, and measuring PSE pathways by evolution metrics to identify emerging, hot and mature pathways. An empirical study in the field of “pre-trained large models” identifies 952 PSE pathways across 28,757 patents, 15 technical problems, 17 technical solutions, and 15 technical effects. We observe solutions addressing “vehicle detection and model redundancy” evolved from simple identification to efficient and intelligent direction, achieving continuous reductions in model complexity, improvements in detection accuracy and real-time performance. The most emerging and hottest pathway (e.g., P2: Complex Medical Decoding Weakness-S3: Multi-Scale Semantic-Prior Fusion-E5: Medical Image Segmentation Optimization), and mature pathways also are identified to help R&D resource distribution. Future research will focus on PSE sub-elements extraction, adaptation to different patent languages and legal jurisdictions, and validation of technological evolution analysis.

title: How external contexts shape research data sharing practices and scholarly impact
abstract: This study examines whether research data-sharing methods differ according to external research factors in a country where open science is still in an early diffusion stage, and whether these factors jointly influence scholarly diffusion outcomes. The dataset consists of Scientific Reports articles (2018–2024) with at least one South Korean–affiliated author. Data-sharing methods were identified through each article’s ‘DAS’, and external factors included ‘Field’, ‘Affiliation’, ‘Author composition’, and ‘Funding’. Scholarly diffusion was measured using ‘Altmetrics’, ‘Usage’, and ‘CNCI’. Multinomial logistic regression was used to analyze determinants of ‘DAS’ selection. Differences in diffusion were evaluated using the Kruskal–Wallis test and Dunn’s test, and interaction effects were examined using linear regression with interaction terms and ANOVA Type II. The results show clear differences in data-sharing practices across external factors. Although ‘upon request’ has become increasingly common, it does not contribute positively to any diffusion metric, performing consistently worse than open data-sharing methods. Short-term diffusion indicators show the most distinct patterns, while medium-term effects appear weaker. Interaction analyses indicate that external factors—particularly ‘Field’ and ‘Funding’—modify the diffusion effects associated with specific ‘DAS’ types. This study provides empirical evidence on data-sharing behavior in an early open-science environment and expands the analytical scope of data-sharing research by linking external factors, data-sharing methods, and diffusion outcomes. The findings suggest actionable implications for promoting data sharing and guiding national or institutional strategies.

title: Does reviewers’ sentiment disagreement during peer review predict novelty and disruption?
abstract: Peer review is a pivotal process in which reviewers provide valuable feedback for scientific research. The role of reviewers during peer review has been at the core of many critical discussions, especially concerning their limited role of merely exhibiting agreement for a submission and their potential failure to assess the “true quality” of research. However, there is limited empirical evidence on the relationship between disagreement among reviewers and novelty or disruption. In this paper, we collect open peer review data comprising 13,952 papers published in Nature Communications and eLife from 2013 to 2021, and study this relationship. Specifically, our results reveal that when measuring the reviewers’ disagreement from a sentimental perspective, the coefficients capturing the relationship between disagreement among reviewers and novelty or disruption are not statistically significant. This finding holds across several robustness checks and when considering the involvement of the number of reviewers during the peer review process. Our empirical analysis suggests that the diversity of opinion among reviewers plays a limited role in identifying substantial novelty or disruptive research. This insight is of vital importance in enhancing the understanding of the role reviewer plays during the peer review process and how their behaviors may impact scientific progress.

title: Are large language models able to predict highly cited papers? Evidence from statistical publications
abstract: Predicting highly cited papers is a persistent challenge owing to delayed citation accumulation and highly skewed impact distributions. This study examines whether large language models (LLMs) can infer long-term citation impact from early-stage textual information. Using a dataset of 90,167 statistical publications from 42 journals spanning 1991–2023, we develop a structured prompt-based framework to evaluate papers across Top 1%, Top 5%, and Top 10% citation thresholds. Across six publication periods, the proposed approach achieves stable but threshold-dependent performance. For the selected primary model, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the average accuracy, recall, and F1 scores are, respectively, 0.879, 0.841, and 0.128 at the Top 1% threshold; 0.892, 0.705, and 0.401 at the Top 5% threshold; and 0.888, 0.582, and 0.513 at the Top 10% threshold. These results demonstrate how predictive performance varies across citation thresholds. Furthermore, repeated inference experiments show agreement rates exceeding 0.94, indicating a high degree of stability. Additional ablation and sensitivity analyses reveal that performance remains stable under the removal of individual metadata fields and controlled rewriting of titles and abstracts, providing evidence against strong dependence on specific inputs or exact textual memorization. Applying the framework to 11,974 recent papers published during 2021–2023, 14.05% are identified as potential high-impact candidates, with thematic concentrations in causal inference, high-dimensional modeling, and machine learning integration. These findings suggest that LLMs can extract meaningful early textual signals associated with future citation impact, providing a scalable and generalizable tool for early-stage research evaluation.

title: Identification and analysis of key and core technologies based on multilayer coupled patent networks
abstract: Identifying key and core technologies (KCTs) is important for governments and industrial decision-makers seeking to promote emerging technologies and foster future industries. The central challenge is to represent the complex interactions among knowledge discovery, technological breakthroughs, and collaborative R&D among innovation actors. From the perspective of multilayer coupled patent networks, this study develops an integrated KCT identification framework centered on fundamental knowledge innovation, technological-principle breakthroughs, and collaborative R&D among innovation actors. To analyze the multilayer coupled network structure, we adapt MRFNL, a joint node-and-layer PageRank algorithm designed for multilayer networks, to estimate interlayer coupling in the three-layer patent network. The resulting layer weights are combined with within-layer degree-centrality and structural-hole measures to construct the technology α-criticality index and the technology β-centrality index. The Criteria Importance Through Intercriteria Correlation (CRITIC) method then provides objective weights for these two indices, yielding the technology γ-key-and-core index used to identify key and core technologies (KCTs). A two-dimensional centrality-criticality plane is then used to examine technology positions, structural characteristics, and structural technology-trend signals. In the empirical application to new-type energy storage, the search results for six technology routes yielded 181,057 raw patent records; after cleaning, 160,320 valid records were retained for model analysis. The model identifies 29 KCT categories and extracts 38 prospective technology signals. Of the 29 identified International Patent Classification (IPC) technology categories, 22 have an adjudicated semantic correspondence with at least one Multi-National Policy-Focused Technology Set (MN-PFTS) policy theme, and 22 of the 39 MN-PFTS themes are covered. Policy-matching precision is 75.86%, MN-PFTS theme recall is 56.41%, and the policy-reference matching harmonic mean is 64.71%. Within the observable scope of patent data, the framework represents coupled relations among fundamental knowledge innovation, technological-principle breakthroughs, and collaborative R&D, broadening the structural representation used to identify key technologies in complex technological systems.

title: Crossing disciplinary borders: how Italian SSH journal rankings address multidisciplinarity
abstract: The classification of Italian academic journals in the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH), carried out by ANVUR (the National Agency for the Evaluation of Universities and Research Institutes), plays a critical role in evaluating research output and shaping academic careers. However, the extent to which this classification adequately accounts for multidisciplinarity—a fundamental aspect of addressing complex societal challenges—remains underexplored. By analysing the Italian classification framework and reviewing journal profiles, we identify systemic biases, disciplinary boundaries, and structural constraints that may hinder the integration of cross-disciplinary scholarship in the Italian academic landscape. Our findings reveal a partial and inconsistent consideration of this dimension, highlighting both recent advancements and persistent limitations in fostering cross-disciplinary collaboration among researchers. This study contributes to the ongoing debate on research evaluation in SSH, offering recommendations to improve classification systems so that they better align with the evolving nature of scholarly inquiry, societal needs, and global research trends.

title: Bibliometric reporting frameworks and the data-cleaning gap: a response to McKay
Expanding bibliometric reporting frameworks to include data preparation practices
Metric capital: how academic indicators become interactional resource
abstract: Abstract This article develops a sociological theory of how academic indicators acquire force in academic life. Based on Randall Collins’s interaction ritual theory, it distinguishes three analytically separate layers that are often conflated in studies of bibliometrics: reception traces, valuation tokens, and metric capital. Academic interactions leave traces in the form of citations, mentions, and article downloads. Selected ones are then stabilized by digital infrastructures, which reduce them to tokens by collecting, certifying, and making them internally comparable. Individual academics accumulate these tokens into a portfolio of objectified symbols that can be mobilized in further interactions—both informally and formally. In this way, they constitute a form of capital. It is activated through three mechanisms. First, it influences the course of interaction before it begins (pre-entrainment), is transferable through structural holes, and also allows for the closure of discussions during evaluation rituals where diverse evaluation cultures or low competence in assessing the quality of work exist. Metric capital can be separated from a scientist’s informal reputation within the scientific community in various ways. The article thus proposes to expand the discussion about measures from the question of what they represent to the question of how they interactively shape the scientific order.

title: Moving towards decolonizing health professions education research: an analysis of global network patterns and equity implications
abstract: Abstract Colonialism has left a lasting remnant in global academic community, with research contributions and authorship historically concentrated among high-income countries. This imbalance has made decolonization in research a global agenda aimed at rebalancing power relations across the community. Nevertheless, traditional bibliometric tools remain unable to capture such underlying power dynamics. This study proposes leveraging social network analysis (SNA) to examine community architecture and promote inclusivity in health professions education (HPE) research. We analyzed peer-reviewed articles published between 2015 and 2024 in leading HPE journals, extracting country-level co-authorship data from Scopus.
