SNA metrics, particularly small world coefficient and centrality, were used to assess collaboration structures, integration patterns, and power dynamics, capturing how power is distributed across the network. The analysis revealed an expanding–centralized pattern: although the research community has expanded globally, with more countries contributing, the overall network structure has remained hierarchical. The network’s small-worldness declined, indicating growing concentration of power within the network core, while stable centrality showed that dominant players have remained consistent throughout the decade. Despite an increasing number of nodes suggesting broader participation, power became increasingly centralized rather than distributed toward the periphery, suggesting the global network remains structurally inequitable and epistemic colonization may still persist. Systemic reforms in research infrastructure, nationally and globally, and in journal policies are needed to enable greater inclusivity. SNA offers critical insight into the structural imbalances that must be monitored to guide process toward achieving an equitable global research ecosystem.

title: Intelligent technological problem–solution recommendation using large language models and heterogeneous graph neural networks
abstract: Technological innovation increasingly depends on the efficient identification and reuse of existing knowledge to address emerging technological problems. However, existing problem–solution recommendation approaches often rely on manual retrieval or document-level similarity, limiting their scalability and ability to capture fine-grained semantic and structural relationships. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes an intelligent technological problem–solution recommendation framework that integrates large language models (LLMs) and heterogeneous graph neural networks. The proposed framework comprises two main stages. First, LLMs are employed to extract and standardize technological problem and solution entities from patent texts, enabling fine-grained entity-level modeling. Based on semantic similarity and co-occurrence relationships, a dynamic bi-layer technological problem–solution network is constructed to represent evolving technological knowledge. Second, the heterogeneous graph neural network model is applied to learn semantic, structural, and temporal representations within the network and to predict potential associations between emerging technological problems and existing solutions. To enhance interpretability, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is incorporated to generate evidence-grounded explanations for recommended matches. A case study in the artificial intelligence domain demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework through quantitative evaluation and qualitative analysis. The results indicate that integrating semantic extraction with dynamic heterogeneous graph modeling significantly improves recommendation performance. This study provides a scalable and data-driven approach for modeling technological knowledge relationships and supporting intelligent technological problem–solution recommendation in evolving innovation systems.

title: From resources to results: how interim outputs improve and mediate R&D output prediction
abstract: Predicting which research and development (R&D) projects will succeed has become a pressing challenge as portfolios expand under finite administrative capacity. Most prediction models rely on features observed at project initiation. They explain neither why certain features predict, nor how their predictive power evolves over the project lifecycle. This study addresses both gaps. We analyse 10,704 government-supported small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) R&D projects in South Korea conducted between 2016 and 2020, with outcomes tracked to 2022. Three nested prediction models progressively incorporate proposal-stage, early-stage, and mid-stage information. Bootstrap mediation analysis examines the hypothesised pathway from resource inputs through interim outputs to final outputs. Three findings follow. First, predictive accuracy jumps sharply at the early-to-mid transition: the area under the curve (AUC) rises by 39.4% for patents and 14.0% for commercialisation output over the proposal-stage model. Gains at other transitions remain modest. Second, interim outputs statistically mediated the resource-to-performance association, with significant indirect effects for both output types. The predictive gain aligns with the conversion of resources into productive activity rather than with incidental association. Third, the relationship between interim and final outputs is non-monotonic. Beyond an inflection point, additional deliverables are associated with declining returns, consistent with resource dilution, coordination costs, and incentive distortion in resource-constrained SME settings. Examining these observations jointly within a single nationwide dataset offers a more complete account of when, why, and within what bounds interim signals improve R&D output prediction.

title: Gendered citation practices in software engineering reference lists: a replication study
abstract: Several studies conducted in different scientific disciplines (e.g., physics and neuroscience) have concluded that researchers belonging to some socio-cultural groups (e.g., women, Black, Hispanic) are usually less cited than other researchers belonging to dominating groups. This is usually due to the presence of citation biases in reference lists. These citation biases towards researchers from some socio-cultural groups may inevitably cause unfairness and inaccuracy in the assessment of articles impact. These citation biases may therefore translate to significant disparities in salaries, promotion, retention, grant funding, awards, collaborative opportunities, and publications. In this paper, we conduct –to the best of our knowledge – the first replication study aiming at analyzing gendered citation practices in the software engineering (SE) literature. Our results show the gendered citation practices adopted in papers published in top SE journals are biased (i.e. men-led papers are overcited while women-led papers are undercited) and driven by homophilic behaviours. Raising awareness on this issue is crucial to foster fairness in gendered citation practices. Our study allows reflecting on gendered citation practices adopted by authors of SE journal papers. Our results also show that some efforts still need to be made to achieve fairness in gendered citation practices used in journal papers published in the SE field. Such efforts may notably consist of the inclusion of citation diversity statements in manuscripts submitted for publication in SE journals. Such efforts may help foster scientific inclusion (e.g., fair representation of scientific contributions) in the SE field.

title: Armenia’s science-policy framework for international collaboration: analysis of bilateral funding schemes and bibliometric trends
abstract: Since independence, Armenia has used international scientific cooperation as an important mechanism for integrating its research system into the global scientific community. This study examines how macro-level science-policy instruments, particularly interstate scientific agreements and bilateral competitive funding schemes, are translated into micro-level research outputs, and assesses the role of bilateral competitions in internationalizing Armenian research. The analysis combines documentary research on interstate agreements and bilateral competitions with bibliometric analysis of Web of Science-indexed publications associated with funded projects. The study identifies 103 international scientific cooperation agreements and 35 bilateral competitions implemented since 2009, which supported 345 projects and resulted in 477 WoS-indexed publications. Of these publications, 76.7% were internationally co-authored, compared with 36.7% among publications without identified grant acknowledgements. The results also reveal substantial concentration across research fields and differences between partners in publication volume and citation impact. The study contributes to the science-policy and scientometric literature by conceptualizing bilateral competitive funding as an intermediate mechanism connecting science diplomacy with researcher-level international collaboration and scientific output. The findings suggest that evaluating bilateral research cooperation requires attention not only to funding and publication volume but also to internationalization, field specialization, partner quality and scientific impact. The Armenian case provides an analytically informative example for other small and resource-constrained research systems seeking to strengthen international scientific integration.

title: A Bayesian Network analysis: how do distinguished scholars enhance the innovation performance?
abstract: The resources and capabilities of distinguished scholars are dynamically matched with the external environment, contributing to the continuous output of innovative knowledge and promoting the effective improvement of scholars’ innovation performance. This paper proposes a big data-driven analysis method and establishes a framework for distinguished scholars based on the three dimensions of environment, individual, and collaborative resources, incorporating six characteristic variables, including innovative atmosphere, extrinsic motivation, knowledge producing, scientific research efficacy, breadth of collaboration, and depth of collaboration. Next, using K-Means clustering, distinguished scholars are categorized into three heterogeneous groups, including motivational, platform-based, and collaborative groups. Finally, Bayesian Networks are constructed for each group to uncover the influence mechanism between characteristic variables and knowledge innovation performance, thereby providing personalized development strategies for distinguished scholars to achieve high-performance goals. The findings reveal that Heterogeneous groups of distinguished scholars exhibit distinct Bayesian network structures, with significantly different impact pathways of characteristic variable combinations on performance. Moreover, knowledge producing serves as a core driver of knowledge innovation performance, demonstrating universal applicability. Furthermore, resource allocation for collaborative partnerships should be differentiated based on scholar types. The motivational group should maintain a moderate breadth of collaboration, while the collaborative group should further expand collaboration channels to stimulate innovation. This paper points out a variety of possible strategies for heterogeneous distinguished scholars to achieve high performance, and highlights the equal utility effect of different characteristic combinations on scholars’ innovation performance, providing theoretical and behavioral guidance for management departments to implement differentiated performance incentive measures.

title: Cardiovascular medicine preprints: publication rates, citation rates, and time to publication
abstract: Preprints are preliminary reports that have not undergone peer review and have seen exponential growth in health sciences, particularly following the COVID-19 pandemic. Preprints facilitate rapid dissemination and scientific discussion. Their role in cardiovascular medicine, a rapidly advancing field, remains incompletely understood. Evaluate the publication rate and the difference in citation counts and citation rates between preprint and published versions of cardiovascular preprints. We collected cardiovascular preprints from two major preprint servers, medRxiv and Research Square, using data scraping and CrossRef metadata. We determined the publication rate and compared citation counts and citation rates using non-parametric methods between the published preprints and their publication version. Additionally, we analyzed the publication rate, citation counts, citation rates, and time interval from preprint posting to journal publication among preprint servers. Among 5625 preprints, 1837 (32.66%) were published in peer-reviewed journals. Older preprints showed higher cumulative publication rates as of the data extraction date, with 61.50% of preprints from 2019 published compared with 6.36% of preprints from 2024 ( p < 0.001). The median time to publication was 154 days, with significant differences between preprint servers (Research Square: 133 days vs. medRxiv: 185 days, p < 0.001). Citation analysis revealed a median of 0 citations for all preprints, with 84.80% having zero citations. Published preprints had significantly higher citation counts than unpublished ones (median 0 vs. 0, p < 0.0001; mean 0.55 vs. 0.25), and published articles had notably more citations than their respective preprints (median 5 vs. 0, p < 0.0001; mean 13.51 vs. 0.55). Published preprints had higher monthly citation rates than unpublished ones, and published articles had higher monthly citation rates than their respective preprints ( p <0.0001). A greater proportion of older cardiovascular preprints had transitioned to peer-reviewed publication by the data extraction date. Preprints that are published receive more citations, suggesting that published versions are perceived as more scientifically impactful.

title: Correction: Will patents with more interdisciplinary scientific knowledge have higher technological impact? Empirical evidence from USPTO patents
When Acknowledgements Don’t Match: Evidence from Horizon 2020
abstract: Abstract Funding acknowledgements have become a valuable data source in recent years. The validity of acknowledgements as indicators of direct project-level support, however, remains contested for several reasons. This study examines the reliability of funding acknowledgement data by comparing publications that acknowledge the European Union’s Horizon 2020 Framework Programme in Scopus with publications officially recorded as project outputs in the CORDIS database. Focusing on social science–related fields, this study conducts aggregate-, project-, and semantic-level analyses to assess the correspondence between acknowledged and administratively recorded funding. The results show a substantial and persistent mismatch: only about half of the publications acknowledging Horizon 2020 funding in Scopus can be linked to a corresponding project in CORDIS. This divergence is persistent over time, occurs across funding instruments and subject areas, and is unlikely to be explained solely by reporting delays, administrative incompleteness, or technical matching limitations alone. Instead, the semantic analysis indicates that many unmatched publications are thematically more distant from the confirmed research core of funded projects, suggesting that funding acknowledgements in bibliographic metadata capture also broader, indirect, or non-project-core relations to funding beyond formally reported project outputs.

title: Measuring research-related academic performance in a comprehensive university: individual heterogeneity, institutional context, and multidimensional output profiles
abstract: Abstract Assessing research-related academic performance remains a central challenge in scientometrics because scholarly output is multidimensional, unevenly distributed across individuals, and embedded in disciplinary and institutional contexts. This study examines the relative contribution of between-individual heterogeneity and institutional context to research-related academic performance in a Romanian comprehensive public university, using a five-year panel dataset comprising 444 academic staff members and 2,220 person-year observations from 2017 to 2021. Performance was measured through two complementary approaches: a relative performance indicator expressing each individual’s annual research score in relation to the benchmark for their current academic position, and a multidimensional activity profile based on 20 research-output indicators. Generalized linear mixed models, exploratory generalized additive models (GAM), and multivariate constrained ordination were used. The most parsimonious mixed model retained year, age, academic title, and study field and yielded a marginal R 2 of 23% and a conditional R 2 of 78%. Constrained ordination showed a similar pattern, with respondent identity explaining 49.79% of adjusted variation in activity profiles. Over time, output profiles shifted toward Q1/Q2 publications and independent citations. In the GAM analysis, work seniority was not associated with relative performance, whereas time since last promotion showed a nonlinear relationship, with performance increasing during the first years after promotion and declining thereafter. Overall, persistent between-individual differences accounted for the largest share of structured variation, while institutional, field-specific, and career-stage factors contributed to differences in the level and composition of academic output.

title: Citation accuracy, citation noise, and citation bias: a foundation of citation analysis
abstract: Abstract Citation analysis is widely used in research evaluation to assess the impact of scientific papers. These analyses rest on the assumption that citation decisions by authors are accurate, representing the flow of knowledge from cited to citing papers. However, in practice, researchers often cite for reasons that are not related to the fact that there has been (intellectual) input from previous papers. Citations made for rhetorical reasons or without reading the cited work compromise the value of citations as instrument for research evaluation. Past research on threats to the accuracy of citations has mainly focused on citation bias as the primary concern. In this paper, we argue that citation noise—the undesirable variance in citation decisions—represents an equally critical but underexplored challenge in citation analysis. We define and differentiate two types of citation noise: citation level noise and citation pattern noise. Each type of noise is described in terms of how it arises and the specific ways it can undermine the validity of citation-based research assessments. By conceptually differing citation noise from citation accuracy and citation bias, we propose a framework for the foundation of citation analysis. We discuss strategies and interventions to minimize citation noise, aiming to improve the reliability and validity of citation analysis in research evaluation. We recommend that the current professional reform movement in research evaluation such as the Coalition for Advancing Research Assessment (CoARA) pick up these strategies and interventions as an additional building block for careful, responsible use of bibliometric indicators in research evaluation.

title: Beyond homogenization in university rankings: a discipline-structure-sensitive evaluation method
abstract: University rankings have become influential instruments of governance in higher education, yet most institution-level systems apply unified indicators and weighting structures to universities with markedly different disciplinary profiles. This can translate disciplinary breadth and greater visibility in metric-intensive fields into structural advantages, while giving less recognition to institutions with concentrated disciplinary strengths. Existing approaches, including subject rankings and classification-based evaluation, provide valuable field-specific or contextualized comparisons, but do not always produce a common institution-level ordering. This study develops a discipline-structure-sensitive method that incorporates disciplinary heterogeneity directly into the aggregation process. Using 141 universities drawn from China’s Double First-Class initiative, the method constructs a continuous disciplinary structure vector, measures each university’s similarity to six disciplinary prototypes, and uses the resulting similarities to combine the performance scores generated by six discipline-specific indicator systems. An attenuation coefficient, λ, regulates the influence of disciplinary distinctiveness on the final ranking. The results show that leading comprehensive universities remain broadly stable, while specialized universities exhibit heterogeneous responses. The largest upward movements occur when a concentrated disciplinary structure coincides with strong relative performance in the structurally dominant discipline. Sensitivity analysis across different values of λ shows that stronger disciplinary weighting gradually reshapes the overall ordering and tier composition, while rankings remain highly stable under adjacent parameter settings and marginal effects diminish at higher values. Methodologically, the framework introduces a continuous and profile-sensitive form of institution-level comparison by allowing disciplinary structure to shape aggregation weights within a common ranking space. Its transparent and adjustable design provides a new way to accommodate disciplinary heterogeneity while preserving comparability across institutions. More broadly, the framework can help reduce incentives for indiscriminate disciplinary expansion, strengthen recognition of distinctive institutional strengths, and promote greater diversity in higher education development.

title: Mutualism in socio-semantic networks: structural correlates of publication output across ecosystem approaches to health
abstract: Abstract While existing scientometric research has examined how individual network position and team composition affect citation-based performance, less is known about how the structural configuration of socio-semantic networks relates to collective publication output. We propose that publication output is associated with configurations that foster mutual visibility between research topics (memes) and author communities. Drawing on mutualistic network theory from ecology, we hypothesise that lower bipartite modularity (H1) and higher nestedness (H2) are associated with higher publication output. We analyse 6,406 publications across three ecosystem approaches to health (EcoHealth, One Health, Planetary Health) over 18 approach × period observations (2004–2023), linking author communities to 20 research topics identified by Latent Dirichlet Allocation. Our analyses show an empirical asymmetry: bipartite modularity is negatively and robustly associated with publication output (Spearman ρ = −0.79, p < 0.001; robust across four community detection algorithms and under leave-one-out by approach), whereas weighted nestedness shows a positive but non-significant association ( ρ = +0.39, p = 0.11), in a direction consistent with H2 but without statistical support at the cell level. The modularity result supports the H1 component of the framework: low modularity — author communities touching multiple topics — fosters mutual visibility between authors and themes. Given the observational design, we report these as field-level patterns, not causal mechanisms. The non-significant association for H2, combined with marked algorithmic variability, invites reconsidering how nestedness is operationalised in socio-semantic contexts. By integrating social and semantic dimensions within a mutualistic framework, this approach complements existing scientometric tools.

title: FOS: a large-scale temporal graph benchmark for scientific interdisciplinary link prediction
abstract: Interdisciplinary connections between scientific fields often develop gradually, and forecasting where new cross-field connections will next arise remains a major challenge. We introduce FOS ( F uture O f S cience), a time-aware, graph-based resource built from the OpenAlex knowledge graph that reconstructs annual co-occurrence graphs spanning 65,027 research sub-fields across 19 general domains over the period 1827–2024. In these graphs, edges denote the co-occurrence of two fields in a single publication and are timestamped with the corresponding publication year; nodes are enriched with semantic embeddings, and edges are characterized by temporal and topological descriptors. We formulate the prediction of new field-pair linkages as a temporal link-prediction task, distinguishing recurrent links from emerging (first-time) links, while explicitly treating first-time co-occurrence as a proxy for interdisciplinary novelty. On a tractable, representative multi-domain evaluation subset of FOS, we benchmark eight temporal graph neural network architectures alongside simple, interpretable baselines under three negative-sampling regimes, and we report performance separately for recurrent and emerging links. Our experiments show that (i) embedding long-form textual descriptions of fields improves prediction accuracy beyond structural signals alone, (ii) distinct model classes exhibit complementary strengths across evaluation regimes, and (iii) predicting emerging links is markedly harder than predicting recurrent links for every model, underscoring the difficulty of forecasting genuine novelty. Illustrative case analyses suggest that a subset of high-confidence predictions correspond to field pairings that subsequently appear in 2025 publications and we present these as qualitative examples. We publicly release the full FOS taxonomy graph, the evaluation subsets, temporal data splits, and evaluation code to establish a reproducible benchmark and a challenging testbed for temporal graph learning on sparse, long-horizon scientific networks.

title: CiteSeq2vec: a framework for citation recommendation via semantic embedding of full-text citation sequences
abstract: Citation recommendation can quickly find supplementary references from a large number of academic papers, making citations more comprehensive and accurate. Current methods often use the reference sequence at the end of a paper to recommend citations, neglecting the actual order and repeated citations within the body text of the paper, both of which are referred to as the “full-text citation sequence.” This leads to the loss of context information around citations. Moreover, current research has not yet fully explored the effects of different full-text citation sequences on citation recommendation. Therefore, this paper proposes a framework for citation recommendation based on semantic embedding of full-text citation sequences. First, we construct multiple types of citation sequences using different strategies to citation order and repeated citations extracted from the full text of the paper. Second, we apply different deep learning methods to generate semantic embedding for each citation using its rich context information. Finally, we compute the semantic similarity between citation embeddings for citation recommendation and evaluate the performance through link prediction. The results in the field of artificial intelligence show that each method achieves the best performance when using citation sequence with repetition (CSR) for citation recommendations. Compared to citation sequences extracted from reference (CSER) and citation sequences without repetition (CSWR), the AUC increased by 15.3% and 12.7%, respectively, while the MAP showed corresponding improvements of 17.7% and 15.8%. In addition, position-sensitive embedding methods consistently outperformed network embedding methods, with NeZha and ALBERT providing the most effective representations for global-level and query-level citation recommendation, respectively. The empirical research results in the field of artificial intelligence show that the actual citation order and repeated citations could provide more accurate and richer contextual information for citation recommendation. Furthermore, using position-sensitive embedding methods is necessary and significantly improves the performance of citation-sequence representations for recommendation.

title: Intelligent patent infringement analysis methods based on patent-function-principle-structure network
abstract: Patent infringement analysis (PIA) is very important to ensure the compliance of product design. However, prevailing methods predominantly rely on post-hoc structural comparisons, which not only contradict the function-oriented paradigm of conceptual design but also prove inadequate for large-scale infringement detection across extensive functional knowledge repositories. To address these limitations, this study proposes an intelligent patent infringement analysis framework based on the patent-function-principle-structure (PFPS) network. First, patent knowledge is extracted and annotated with infringement risk labels according to claims to construct the PFPS network. Second, a morphological matrix linking functional requirements to functional knowledge nodes is established; guided by the all-elements rule, hash functions are employed for preliminary screening of node combinations, followed by a hybrid similarity metric to identify potential equivalent infringement risks. Third, criteria derived from the reverse doctrine of equivalents are integrated to regulate the function-principle-structure mapping process, thereby enabling systematic patent design-around. Finally, the feasibility of the proposed method is validated through a case study on an irregular workpiece transfer device. Results demonstrate that the method effectively makes up for the shortcomings of infringement analysis and design-around within patent knowledge-driven conceptual design.

title: Why retracted papers continue to be cited: direct survey evidence complements citation-pattern analysis
The open catalogue of global scientific academies: organizational identity, web presence, and scholarly communication infrastructure
abstract: Scientific academies play long-standing roles in scholarly recognition, science advice, public communication, and knowledge dissemination, yet comparable evidence about these organizations remains fragmented across open registries, institutional websites, and bibliographic authority systems. This paper introduces an open catalogue of global scientific academies that integrates three linked evidence layers: organizational identity, public-facing web presence, and academy-linked scholarly communication infrastructure, operationalized through journal records. The identity layer represents academies as persistent organizational entities and connects them to open registries and knowledge bases through stable identifiers and validated cross-system mappings. The web layer uses navigation menus, sitemap-derived URL hierarchies, Formal Concept Analysis, and graph pruning to construct a shared taxonomy of academy website functions, supporting comparative analysis of web-structural patterns, imitation, and differentiation. The bibliographic layer links academies to Zeitschriftendatenbank records through curated corporate-body authority mappings and uses journal title histories to examine the right-censored lifecycles of observable academy-linked journals. The analysis shows that registry identifiers provide uneven but informative evidence for organizational identity anchoring, and that academy websites differ in the functional structures through which governance, communication, cooperation, and knowledge resources are made visible. Academy-linked journal records further document historically layered journal title trajectories, with uneven observability and persistence across institutional contexts. By treating organizational records, website structures, and journal title histories as distinct but linkable evidence, the catalogue provides a reusable data foundation for comparative research on scientific academies across heterogeneous open research information systems.

title: Decoding funded research: comparative analysis of topic models and uncovering the effect of gender and geographic location
abstract: Optimizing national scientific investment requires a clear understanding of evolving research trends and the demographic and geographical forces shaping them, particularly in light of commitments to equity, diversity, and inclusion. To address this need, we analyzed 18 years (2005–2022) of research proposals funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC). We conducted a comprehensive comparative evaluation of three topic modelling approaches: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), Structural Topic Modelling (STM), and BERTopic. We also introduced a novel algorithm, named COFFEE, designed to enable robust estimation of covariate associations for BERTopic. This advancement addresses a significant gap, as BERTopic lacks a native function for covariate analysis, unlike probabilistic STM. Our findings highlight that while all models effectively delineate core scientific domains, BERTopic exhibited greater thematic granularity and contextual sensitivity than LDA and STM by consistently identifying more granular, coherent, and emergent topics, such as the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence. Additionally, the covariate analysis, powered by COFFEE, identified distinct provincial research specializations and consistent gender-based thematic differences across various scientific disciplines. These insights offer a robust empirical foundation for funding organizations to formulate more equitable and impactful funding strategies, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of the scientific ecosystem.

title: Regional disparities in the research productivity of returned scholars in Chinese universities
abstract: Hiring faculty who hold doctoral degrees from foreign institutions, commonly referred to as returned scholars, has become increasingly common among universities in emerging economies. This study examines the research output of returned scholars employed at Chinese universities across three geographic-economic regions: Eastern, Central, and Western China. Using a dataset covering 233 returned scholars in the business schools of first-tier Chinese universities, we find that scholars in the Central region exhibit significantly lower academic output quality than those in the Eastern and Western regions. This non-monotonic pattern does not follow the conventional East-to-West economic gradient. We further examine this regional disparity through international and domestic collaboration, treated as proxies for returned scholars’ human and social capital, and find that these collaboration patterns are associated with the observed productivity differences. The pattern also varies across business schools: the Central-region disadvantage is attenuated in less prestigious schools and in those with greater openness. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the relationship between returned scholars’ career location and research productivity while accounting for both individual and institutional characteristics. Our findings carry policy implications for mitigating regional disparities and supporting the research productivity of overseas returnees.

title: Is reviewer recognition associated with labor input? A large-scale analysis of PLoS One peer review reports and CRediT
abstract: Research input–output relations shape scientific research patterns. Moving beyond conventional citation-based studies, this paper investigates the association between labor input and reviewer recognition from the peer review perspective. This study adopts an observational and correlational design, selecting 26,775 PLoS One publications (2019–2024) with both peer review reports and CRediT contribution statements as research samples. Employing descriptive statistics and correlation analysis, it explores how labor input relates to reviewer recognition level and consensus level across four dimensions: Methodology, Analysis, Data and Writing. The main results are as follows. First, the association between labor input and reviewer recognition varies across research activity types. Writing features “high labor input, high recognition, high consensus”, showing a tendency of “more effort, more gain”; Analysis shows relatively “low labor input, high recognition, low consensus”, reflecting the professionalism and subjective variability in the evaluation part. Second, interaction effects exist among different research activities: increased labor input in Writing is significantly yet weakly positively correlated with higher recognition level in Methodology, which tentatively implies that Writing serves as an integrated and visible research activity. Third, the US, UK and Japan generally conform to the overall observed patterns, while China appears to show divergent features. Specifically, China seems to have higher labor input accompanied by lower recognition and greater controversy in Writing, and lower labor input alongside higher recognition and less controversy in Analysis. From a fine-grained perspective of scientific research activities, this paper provides tentative empirical evidence for understanding the input–output research patterns, as well as revealing the organizational efficiency of academic labor division. This study has limitations including reliance on single data source, unconsidered reviewer differences and the absence of causal inference.

title: Institutional visibility and professional participation of industrial bioengineers: evidence from Japan’s professional engineer system
abstract: Industrial biotechnology plays a central role in contemporary socio-technical systems, yet the institutional visibility of industrial bioengineers within professional qualification systems remains poorly understood. This study combines a comparative review of international engineering qualification frameworks with quantitative analysis of membership statistics from Japan’s Professional Engineer system to examine how industrial bioengineering is represented within engineering professions. The review indicates that bioengineering is frequently positioned within biomedical engineering, whereas explicit qualification categories encompassing genetic engineering, cell engineering, and industrial bioprocess engineering remain uncommon internationally. Quantitative analysis across 20 engineering disciplines identified a significant negative association between division size and membership rate in an overdispersion-adjusted binomial model, although complementary analyses indicated that the strength of this relationship depended partly on the analytical treatment of divisions and the influence of individual large divisions. In contrast, the biotechnology division exhibited both the highest membership rate (59.4%) and the highest female representation (13.4%) among all divisions. These findings suggest that disciplinary communities characterized by rapid technological change and continuing ethical and regulatory challenges may sustain stronger professional participation than expected from division size alone. By integrating institutional comparison with quantitative analysis of professional communities, this study contributes to understanding how emerging technological fields are represented, organized, and sustained within engineering qualification systems.

title: The dynamic evolution and trend forecasting of disruptive innovation in China: an empirical study based on patent data
abstract: Advancing research on disruptive innovation has become an urgent and significant challenge for the academic community. Due to the constraints of existing research perspectives, most studies predominantly focus on uncovering the conditions for the emergence of disruptive innovation and its micro-level impacts, which limits a comprehensive understanding of its development from a macro perspective. This study constructs a quantitative analytical framework to assess the disruptive technological innovation levels across industries, regions, and firms. It examines the spatiotemporal evolution of regional disruptive technological innovation in China from 2008 to 2022, and conducts trend forecasting and factor analysis. The key findings are as follows. (1) The level of disruptive technological innovation in China shows an upward trend but remains relatively low. State-owned enterprises demonstrate superior innovation levels compared to non-state-owned enterprises. At the industry level, sectors such as information and communication technology, high-end equipment manufacturing, and new energy have shown remarkable growth. (2) There are significant regional disparities in China’s disruptive technological innovation. The dynamic evolution of disruptive innovation is a gradual process characterized by stability and a propensity for upward transitions. Trend forecasting indicates the presence of a Matthew Effect in regional disruptive innovation levels. (3) Variables such as the number of higher education institutions, economic development level, degree of openness, R&D investment intensity, and financial development significantly contribute to enhancing the disruptive innovation level across provinces, whereas per capita capital stock has a negative impact. Based on these findings, reducing regional disparities in disruptive innovation levels and promoting balanced regional economic development require tailored innovation strategies. Policies should account for regional development stages and temporal evolution, providing differentiated support to regions based on their unique circumstances. The results of this study contribute to the cultivation of disruptive technological innovation and offer insights for advancing the development of new-quality productive forces.

title: Patent strategies under different innovation modes: a comparative analysis of FDA-approved blockbuster drugs using Orange Book and USPTO data
abstract: This study aims to bridge this gap by examining how different research and development innovation models—classified based on patent ownership—are associated with distinct patent strategies and market outcomes. We conducted a drug-level analysis of 151 blockbuster drugs by integrating data from PharmaCompass, the FDA Orange Book, and the USPTO. Based on the ultimate ownership of 1,176 core patents, we classify each drug’s development into one of four models: Closed Innovation (21.85%), Contract-based OI (30.46%), Coopetition-based OI (32.45%), and Network-based OI (15.23%), with open innovation collectively accounting for 78.15% of the sample. We then compared these models across six patentometric indicators. Our results reveal that the adoption of innovation models has significantly evolved over time. More importantly, we identify four unique patent strategy profiles: Network-OI possesses the most extensive patent portfolio and the longest duration for market entry. Conversely, Contract-OI facilitates the most rapid market entry, albeit with the least robust patent protection. Closed Innovation pursues aggressive patenting both before and after drug approval, while Coopetition-OI achieves notably extended market exclusivity through strategic patent portfolio management, leveraging a relatively large patent portfolio and an extended patent active period. This study illustrates how the selection of an R&D innovation model influences a firm’s patenting behavior and its capacity to capture value, presenting significant theoretical and managerial implications.

title: Response to “Why retracted papers continue to be cited: direct survey evidence complements citation-pattern analysis”
Do awards make scholars shine brighter? The halo effect on research career in Taiwan
abstract: Abstract Research award winners are often believed to benefit from a halo effect. While previous empirical studies support the idea that receiving a research award helps increase funding, this causal relationship has been proven through comparisons between awardees and non-awardees. This study aims to explore the direct impact of the halo effect on awardees themselves, focusing on the ego-Matthew effect , the Pygmalion effect , and social capital , rather than comparing them to non-awardees. Specifically, it explores whether receiving a research award enhances an awardee’s ability to secure funding, improve research output, and expand collaboration opportunities. The study analyzes data from 122 national scientific research award winners in the Management discipline in Taiwan from 2011 to 2017, tracking their research performance four years before and after receiving the award. In addition, considering that the outstanding research awards are divided into senior and junior categories, this study also compares the benefits of receiving the award between senior and junior awardees. The findings reveal that while research awards increase funding opportunities for younger awardees and facilitate international and cross-disciplinary collaboration for senior awardees, they do not significantly enhance an awardee’s own research output. These insights contribute to both theoretical and practical discussions on the long-term impact of research recognition in academia.

title: Network position and scientific recognition: author centrality and citation outcomes in top AI conferences
abstract: Abstract This study investigates how authors' structural positions within scientific collaboration networks drive citation disparities beyond research content. We analyze 17,942 papers from three top AI conferences (NeurIPS, ICLR and ICML) spanning 2005 to 2024. To address the limitations of existing metrics, we introduce a novel centrality measure, HCTCD, which incorporates temporal decay and collaboration intensity. To isolate the effect of network structure, we rigorously control for textual content via a pre-trained transformer encoder. The relationship is then modeled using Beta regression, with the citation percentile within each publication year as the dependent variable. Our results demonstrate that long-term centrality exerts a stronger influence than short-term metrics. Critically, team-level centrality aggregation outperforms author-rank approaches. Furthermore, after controlling for content and other variables, incorporating a co-author with centrality 50\% higher than the first author is associated with a significant increase in expected citations, illustrating a clear “social lift”. These findings underscore the primacy of collective network connectivity and advocate for network-aware evaluation to mitigate structural inequities in scientific recognition.

title: The representation of SDG-related research in bibliometric databases: persisting imbalances and varying perspectives
abstract: Abstract The societal impact of research has become an explicit goal of research activities and argument for the funding of the science system. Providers of bibliometric databases algorithmically assign scientific publications to SDG goals to show how single research outputs contribute to society, but substantial disagreements among these classifications have been quantified. Moreover, large language models (LLMs) are being introduced as a technology that processes scholarly records. We apply LLMs to observe what type of research is assigned to SDGs by these automatic procedures and what structural differences emerge. To this end, we fine-tune in parallel three generic LLMs by SDG-classified abstracts in the databases Web of Science, Scopus and OpenAlex and apply the same prompts to the differently fine-tuned LLMs. Five SDGs are being analyzed - three related to social equity and two to economic and technological development. A human-feedback-driven analysis of the generated noun phrases reveals that the LLM-mediated SDG-classified research information fails to represent the most disadvantaged populations, the poorest countries, and underrepresented topics that SDG targets explicitly address, while economic superpowers in the Global North stay very visible. These paradoxical findings indicate the systemic discrimination against marginalized groups operated by the LLM technology within conventional bibliometric classification frameworks, challenging their assumed neutrality, and question the current visibility of the societal impact of research.

title: Marebito: citation matching interface for the digital library zbMATH open
abstract: Abstract zbMATH Open is a leading curated bibliographic database covering approximately five million publications in mathematics. This paper presents Marebito, a production citation-matching system developed for zbMATH Open, and documents its architecture, domain-adapted feature design, and operational performance at scale. Marebito combines bibliographic parsing with GROBID, candidate retrieval with Elasticsearch, and a supervised Random Forest trained on domain-specific string-similarity features. Evaluation on internal zbMATH Open datasets yields precision and recall exceeding 98% on modern DOI-indexed records. Evaluation across two bibliographically distinct subsets reveals that classifier performance is strongly conditioned on metadata completeness, particularly title and author string quality, rather than DOI availability alone, documenting a concrete challenge for citation matching in mathematical literature. A preliminary comparison with Crossref on a manually verified subset of 2,037 entries illustrates the limitations of general-purpose matchers on specialist mathematical bibliography. A neural reranking baseline confirms that Elasticsearch-derived hard negatives are essential for abstention. We also discuss downstream bibliometric applications within zbMATH Open.

title: The geography of disruption: how disruptive knowledge reaches farther
abstract: Is the character of scientific knowledge related to how far its influence travels? Research on the geography of science has long documented that citation concentrates near its origin, while research on disruption has learned to distinguish papers that overturn existing lines of work from those that consolidate them. The two literatures have developed in parallel, leaving open a basic question: are disruptive and consolidating contributions received across space in the same way? This study connects the two by asking whether a paper’s Disruption Index predicts the geographic distribution of the citations it subsequently receives. Drawing on large-scale bibliometric data covering approximately 656,000 journal articles published in 2015 and seventeen million cited–citing pairs, the analysis traces each paper’s citations through the distance between the cities of the cited and citing teams. Within journals, and conditional on field, country, and team characteristics, more disruptive papers are cited from systematically farther away: a one-standard-deviation increase in disruption corresponds to a 9.0% longer median citation distance and a smaller share of citations from the paper’s own city, and the median distance rises by 25.1% from the most consolidating to the most disruptive quartile of the sample. The pattern holds across fields, replicates in adjacent publication cohorts, and persists when the index is fixed before the outcome citations arrive. Disruptive knowledge thus reaches a geographically wider audience than consolidating knowledge. This regularity matters for how localized knowledge spillovers, and the cluster policies built on them, are understood.

title: A method for assisting latecomers in quickly identifying technology opportunities from public domain patents
abstract: Technology opportunity analysis (TOA) is an important precondition for the successful implementation of technological innovation activities, and is the basis for the latecomers to realize technological catch-up and expand the scale of market share. While there has been much research on finding technological opportunities from patents, little academic attention has been paid to public domain patents as a source of technological opportunities, but the reality is that the technical information disclosed in public domain patent documents is publicly available and may be used without paying royalties to the original patentee, potentially reducing licensing costs; however, freedom to implement any specific technology must be confirmed through legal clearance. They can generate new value when effectively adopted, combined with other technologies, or further commercialized by subsequent innovators. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel approach to assist latecomers in quickly identifying technology opportunities from public domain patents. Firstly, by defining key issues based on user needs, we effectively identify product development opportunities. Secondly, we specifically construct an indicator system for identifying high-value public domain patents and validate its alignment with patent value using Pearson’s correlation coefficient. Finally, by integrating the BERT-LSTM model with SAO semantic analysis, we achieve automatic classification of the SAO structure, ultimately resulting in a three-tier technology map encompassing user needs, key technologies, and technical solutions. This approach, when applied to bio-cosmetic products, demonstrates that public domain patents, particularly expired patents, hold significant potential in reducing R&D costs and the need for licensing, allowing latecomers to identify and assimilate valuable technical knowledge, thereby fostering innovation and driving economic growth.

title: Gender differences in international research collaboration in European Union
abstract: This paper investigates International Research Collaboration (IRC) among European Union (EU) countries from 2011 to 2022, with an emphasis on gender-based authorship patterns. Drawing from the Web of Science Social Science Citation Index (WoS-SSCI) database, a large dataset of IRC articles was constructed, annotated with categories of authorship based on gender and author affiliation. Using network science, the study maps collaboration structures and reveals gendered differences in co-authorship networks. Re-sults highlight a substantial rise in IRC over the decade, particularly with the USA and China as key non-EU partners. Articles with at least one female author were consistently less frequent than those with at least one male author. Notably, female-exclusive collab-orations showed distinctive network topologies, with more centralized (star-like) patterns and shorter tree diameters.

title: RLRMCNW: Research leadership recommendation in research leading-participating multiplex co-author networks based on Wasserstein distance
abstract: Abstract Effective research leadership recommendation is crucial for forming impactful teams, yet existing methods overlook research leadership dynamics and inadequately measure interlayer similarity of multiplex network layers. In this paper, we propose \(\:RMNW\), a novel model for recommending research leadership relationships (leading-leading, leading-participating) using a two-layer multiplex network: a target layer (research leadership) and an auxiliary layer (participating-participating). The \(\:RMNW\) quantifies interlayer similarity via Wasserstein Distance applied to the distributions of nodes’ local and global neighborhoods, capturing structural alignment beyond simple centrality correlations. It integrates target and auxiliary layer information using a tunable parameter (\(\:\lambda\:\)). Evaluated on 426708 publications in Pharmaceutical Sciences (30286 authors), 52381 publications in Information Science & Library Science (6853 authors), and 173264 publications in Computer Sciences (18382 authors). The \(\:RMNW\) significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Key results include: 2.42% higher \(\:F1@7\), 4.63% higher \(\:MRR\) and 4.7% higher \(\:nDCG\:\)than the best baseline (\(\:MALM\)) in Pharmaceutical Sciences. Optimal performance at \(\:\lambda\:\)=0.5, demonstrating the critical role of auxiliary layer information (performance drops 36–46% without it). Superiority over variants using degree-correlation (\(\:RMN{W}_{DDC}\)), neighbor-overlap (\(\:RMN{W}_{ASSN}\)), or link-overlap (\(\:RMN{W}_{LO}\)), confirming Wasserstein Distance’s effectiveness. The \(\:RMNW\) enables precise leader/participant selection for researchers, enhances institutional network growth, and informs funding allocation.
